*Ya'ayyuha al-ladhina amanu la tattakhidhu 'aduwwi wa-'aduwwakum awliya'...*

The verb *ittakhadha* ("to take") is transitive to its two objects, which are *'aduwwi* ("My enemy") and *awliya'* ("allies"). *Al-'aduww* is of the form *fa'ul*, from *'adā*, like *'afuww* from *'afā*. Because it is on the pattern of the verbal noun, it is used for the plural as it is for the singular.

If you ask: with what is *tulqūna* ("you convey") connected? I answer: it may be connected to *la tattakhidhu* as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its implied subject, and *awliya'* is a qualifier of it. It may also be a fresh sentence (*isti'naf*).

If you ask: when you make it a qualifier of *awliya'*, and it has been applied to something other than its referent, where is the pronoun that must appear, which is in your saying *tulqūna ilayhim antum bil-mawaddah* ("you convey to them, you, with affection")? I answer: that is required only of nouns, not of verbs. If it were said *awliya'an mulqina ilayhim bil-mawaddah* as a descriptive, the explicit pronoun would have been necessary. But *al-ilqa'* ("conveying") is an expression for communicating affection and disclosing it to them. It is said *alqa ilayhi khurashay sadrihi* ("he conveyed to him the scum of his chest"), and *afda ilayhi bi-qushurihi* ("he disclosed to him its husks"). [[Your saying "it is said alqa ilayhi khurashay sadrihi" – in al-Sihah (of al-Jawhari): "al-kharsha'" is like al-hirba': the skin of a snake and the shell of an egg after what is in it has come out; then everything that is swollen and hardened like foam is likened to it, and phlegm is sometimes called kharsha'. It is said: alqa khurashay sadrihi. (Editor)]]

As for *bil-mawaddah* ("with affection"), the *ba'* is either superfluous, emphasizing the transitivity, as in *wa-la tulqu bi-aydikum ila al-tahlukah* ("and do not cast yourselves with your own hands into destruction"), or it is original, on the basis that the object of *tulqūna* is omitted, meaning: "you convey to them the news of the Messenger of Allah because of the affection between you and them." Likewise His saying *tusirrūna ilayhim bil-mawaddah* means: "you disclose to them your affection in secret," or "you confide to them the secret of the Messenger of Allah because of the affection."

If you ask: *wa-qad kafarū* ("while they have disbelieved") is a circumstantial clause of what? I answer: either of *la tattakhidhū*, or of *tulqūna*, meaning: do not take them as allies, or love them, while this is their state. *Yukhrijūna* ("they expel") is a fresh sentence, serving as an explanation of their disbelief and their defiance. Or it is a circumstantial clause of *kafarū*.

*An tu'minū* ("that you believe") is the causal explanation of *yukhrijūna*, meaning: they expel you because you believe. *In kuntum kharajtum* ("if you have gone forth") is connected to *la tattakhidhū*, meaning: do not ally with My enemies, if you are My allies. The grammarians' saying about such a construction is that it is a conditional whose answer is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. *Tusirrūna* ("you confide in secret") is a fresh sentence, and its meaning is: what benefit do you have in your secret, when you know that concealment and disclosure are the same in My knowledge, with no difference between them, and that I inform My Messenger of what you conceal? *Wa-man yafalhu* ("and whoever does it") means: whoever does this secret conveying has indeed strayed from the path of truth and right.

Al-Jahdari read *lamma jā'akum* ("when there came to you"), meaning: they disbelieved on account of what came to you, in the sense that they made into a cause of their disbelief what ought to have been the cause of their belief.

*In yathqafūkum* ("if they overcome you") means: if they prevail over you and gain power over you, *yakūnū lakum a'da'an* ("they will be enemies to you") with pure enmity, and will not be allies to you as you are to them, *wa-yabsutū ilaykum aydiyahum wa-alsinatahum bil-su'* ("and will extend to you their hands and tongues with evil"), by killing and insult, and they wish that you would revert from your religion. Therefore, to show affection to such people and to counsel them is a great error on your part and a deception of yourselves. Similar is His saying: *la ya'lunakum khabalan* ("they spare no effort to corrupt you").

If you ask: how does He introduce the answer to the condition in the present tense like the protasis, then say *wa-waddū* ("and they wished") in the past tense? I answer: although the past tense in the conditional construction runs in the manner of the present tense in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis), there is a subtle point in it, as if it were said: they wished, before everything, for your disbelief and apostasy. That is, they wish to inflict upon you the harms of the world and the religion together: the killing of souls, the tearing of honour, and returning you as unbelievers. Returning you as unbelievers is the foremost and first of harms in their view, because they know that religion is dearer to you than your lives, since you sacrifice your lives for it. And the enemy's greatest concern is to target what is most precious to his opponent.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 60, verse 4–5:

It is also read "uswa" and "iswa". It is a noun for the one who is taken as an example (al-mu'tasa bihi), meaning: there was among them a good and approved course of action, such that they could be taken as an example and their traces followed. This was their saying to the disbelievers of their people what they said, when they openly showed enmity to them, bared the stick (qashsharu lahum al-'asa), displayed hatred and detestation, and declared plainly that the cause of their enmity and hatred was nothing but their disbelief in God. As long as this cause remained, the enmity remained; but if they removed it and believed in God alone, the enmity turned into friendship, the hatred into love, and the detestation into affection [[His saying "and al-maqt is maqqa" means: love. (ʿAyn)]]. Thus they made clear their pure sincerity. The meaning of ﴿We disbelieve in you and in what you worship besides God﴾ is: we do not regard your affairs, nor the affairs of your gods, and you are nothing in our estimation.

If you say: with what is the exception ﴿except the saying of Abraham﴾ connected? I say: with the phrase ﴿a good example﴾, because by "the good example" he meant their saying, which it was incumbent upon them to take as an example and to adopt as a practice to follow. If you say:

If His saying ﴿"I will certainly ask forgiveness for you"﴾ is an exception from the saying which is a good example, then what of His saying ﴿"And I possess nothing for you against God in any respect"﴾, which is not fit to be an exception? Do you not see His saying: ﴿Say: "Who possesses anything against God?"﴾ I say: he intended the exception of the whole statement to his father, the intent being the promise of asking forgiveness for him, and what follows is grounded upon it and subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and within my capacity is only asking forgiveness." If you say: with what is His saying ﴿"Our Lord, upon You we have relied"﴾ connected? I say: with what precedes the exception, and it is part of the good example. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "Say, Our Lord," as a command from God to the believers to say it, and as His instruction to them, completing what He enjoined upon them of cutting off ties between them and the disbelievers, and following Abraham and his people in disassociating from them, and as a reminder to turn back to God and seek refuge in Him from the trial of the people of disbelief, and to seek forgiveness for what had passed from them. It is also read "bura'a" like "shuraka'", and "bara'" like "zuraf", and "bara'" by replacing the kasra with a damma, like "rukhal" and "rabab" [[His saying "like rukhal and rabab": in al-Sihah, al-rakhl (with kasra on the kha') is the female of the young of sheep, and the male is hamal; its plural is rukhal, and also rukhal with damma. Also in it: "al-ruba" with damma on the form fu'la: the ewe that has recently given birth; its plural is rabab with damma. (ʿAyn)]], as an adjective used as a verbal noun (waṣf bi-l-maṣdar). And "al-bara'" and "al-bara'a" are like "al-zama'" and "al-zama'a".

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 60, verse 4–5:

It is also read "uswa" and "iswa". It is a noun for the one who is taken as an example (al-mu'tasa bihi), meaning: there was among them a good and approved course of action, such that they could be taken as an example and their traces followed. This was their saying to the disbelievers of their people what they said, when they openly showed enmity to them, bared the stick (qashsharu lahum al-'asa), displayed hatred and detestation, and declared plainly that the cause of their enmity and hatred was nothing but their disbelief in God. As long as this cause remained, the enmity remained; but if they removed it and believed in God alone, the enmity turned into friendship, the hatred into love, and the detestation into affection [[His saying "and al-maqt is maqqa" means: love. (ʿAyn)]]. Thus they made clear their pure sincerity. The meaning of ﴿We disbelieve in you and in what you worship besides God﴾ is: we do not regard your affairs, nor the affairs of your gods, and you are nothing in our estimation.

If you say: with what is the exception ﴿except the saying of Abraham﴾ connected? I say: with the phrase ﴿a good example﴾, because by "the good example" he meant their saying, which it was incumbent upon them to take as an example and to adopt as a practice to follow. If you say:

If His saying ﴿"I will certainly ask forgiveness for you"﴾ is an exception from the saying which is a good example, then what of His saying ﴿"And I possess nothing for you against God in any respect"﴾, which is not fit to be an exception? Do you not see His saying: ﴿Say: "Who possesses anything against God?"﴾ I say: he intended the exception of the whole statement to his father, the intent being the promise of asking forgiveness for him, and what follows is grounded upon it and subordinate to it, as if he said: "I will ask forgiveness for you, and within my capacity is only asking forgiveness." If you say: with what is His saying ﴿"Our Lord, upon You we have relied"﴾ connected? I say: with what precedes the exception, and it is part of the good example. It is also permissible that the meaning be: "Say, Our Lord," as a command from God to the believers to say it, and as His instruction to them, completing what He enjoined upon them of cutting off ties between them and the disbelievers, and following Abraham and his people in disassociating from them, and as a reminder to turn back to God and seek refuge in Him from the trial of the people of disbelief, and to seek forgiveness for what had passed from them. It is also read "bura'a" like "shuraka'", and "bara'" like "zuraf", and "bara'" by replacing the kasra with a damma, like "rukhal" and "rabab" [[His saying "like rukhal and rabab": in al-Sihah, al-rakhl (with kasra on the kha') is the female of the young of sheep, and the male is hamal; its plural is rukhal, and also rukhal with damma. Also in it: "al-ruba" with damma on the form fu'la: the ewe that has recently given birth; its plural is rabab with damma. (ʿAyn)]], as an adjective used as a verbal noun (waṣf bi-l-maṣdar). And "al-bara'" and "al-bara'a" are like "al-zama'" and "al-zama'a".

Then he repeated the exhortation to follow the example of Ibrahim and his people, establishing and emphasizing it for them. That is why it came introduced by an oath, since an oath is the utmost in emphasis. He also substituted for his words "for you" (lakum) the words "for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day" (liman kana yarjul-laha wal-yawmal-akhir), and he followed it with His words, ﴿And whoever turns away, then indeed God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy﴾. Thus he left no kind of emphasis unused, but brought it.

When these verses were revealed, the believers became especially firm in their enmity toward their fathers, their sons, and all their relatives among the polytheists, and in severing ties with them. When Allah, mighty and majestic is He, saw from them such earnestness and patience, in the most intense form, and such prolonged longing for the cause that would permit them to befriend and maintain ties with them, He had mercy on them and promised them the facilitation of what they had wished for. When the conquest of Mecca was made easy, Allah granted them their wish, their people embraced Islam, and there came about between them the love and purity of relations that came about.

It is also said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Umm Habibah, and at that the stubbornness of Abu Sufyan softened and his resistance in enmity loosened. Umm Habibah had embraced Islam and emigrated with her husband Abdullah ibn Jahsh to Abyssinia. He became a Christian and tried to make her Christian too, but she refused and remained steadfast in her religion. Her husband died, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to the Negus and proposed marriage to her through him. [[This is how al-Tha'labi mentioned it, without a chain of narration, and its pieces are scattered across various reports. Abu Dawud and al-Hakim narrated, through al-Zuhri from Urwah from Umm Habibah, that "she was married to Abdullah ibn Jahsh, and he died in the land of Abyssinia. The Negus then married her to the Prophet (ﷺ) and gave her dowry of four thousand on his behalf, and sent her to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with Shurahbil ibn Hasanah." Al-Hakim also narrated from al-Zuhri who said, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Umm Habibah bint Abi Sufyan. She had previously been married to Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, who had emigrated with her from Mecca to Abyssinia, then he was tried, became a Christian, and died a Christian, while Allah kept Islam firm for Umm Habibah until she returned to Medina. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proposed to her, and Uthman ibn Affan married her to him." Al-Zuhri said, "They claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to the Negus, and he married her to him and paid on his behalf forty uqiyyah." Al-Waqidi narrated in al-Maghazi, and through him al-Hakim, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father who said, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Amr ibn Umayyah to the Negus to propose to Umm Habibah on his behalf, and he gave her a dowry of four hundred dinars from his own wealth." Al-Waqidi said: Abdullah ibn Ja'far narrated to me from Abd al-Wahid ibn Abi Awn, who said: When the marriage of the Prophet (ﷺ) to his daughter reached Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, he said, "That is the stallion whose nose is not restrained." Abu Nu'aym said in al-Dala'il, "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Amr ibn Umayyah al-Damri to the Negus, and he married him Umm Habibah bint Abi Sufyan and gave her dowry on his behalf, four hundred dinars, and sent her to him." He said: This was in the sixth year after the Hijrah, after his return from Khaybar, and I know of no disagreement about that.]] and he paid her dowry of four hundred dinars on his behalf. When this reached her father, he said: "That is the stallion whose nose is not restrained." [[His saying "that is the stallion whose nose is not restrained" means that he is not struck on the nose and is not held back, because of his nobility. Reported by al-Sihah. (Gh)]]. "And perhaps" is a promise from Allah in the manner of kings, who say in some matters, "perhaps" or "maybe," so that no doubt remains for the one in need regarding its fulfillment. Or it was intended to raise the hopes of the believers, and Allah is capable of turning hearts, changing conditions, and facilitating the causes of affection. "And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" to whoever among the polytheists embraces Islam.

The Qur'anic phrase أَنْ تَبَرُّوهُمْ is in apposition to الذين لم يقاتلوكم. Likewise, أَنْ تَوَلَّوْهُمْ is in apposition to الذين قاتلوكم.

The meaning: He does not forbid you from being kind to those, but He forbids you from allying yourselves with these. This is also a mercy toward them, given their intense hostility and zeal against you, and it precedes His mercy in facilitating the Islam of their people. He permitted you to maintain relations with those among them who did not openly fight the believers or expel them from their homes.

It was said that He meant by them the tribe of Khuza'a, who had made a treaty with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that they would not fight him or assist anyone against him. It is also related from Mujahid: "They are those who believed in Mecca but did not emigrate."

It was said: "They are the women and the children." It was also said: Qutayla bint Abd al-Uzza, the mother of Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who was a polytheist, came to her with gifts, but Asma' did not accept them and did not permit her to enter. So the verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded her to let her mother enter, to accept from her, to honor her, and to be good to her. [[Al-Hakim related it through al-Mubarak, from Mus'ab ibn Thabit, from Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: "Qutayla bint Abd al-Uzza came to her daughter Asma' bint Abi Bakr, may Allah be pleased with them both. Abu Bakr had divorced her," and he mentioned it and related it more completely.

Through this same chain, Ahmad, al-Bazzar, Abu Dawud, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari, al-Tabarani, Ibn Abi Hatim, and others related it. The hadith of Asma' is in the two Sahihs, from Urwa, from her, with a different context.]]

It is related from Qatada: it was abrogated by the verse of fighting. And act justly toward them: ﴿and deal with them justly﴾, and do not wrong them.

It is enough of a warning that Allah commanded the believers to practice justice toward the polytheists who associate others with Him, and to avoid wronging them. This is a reproach to a Muslim who dares to wrong his fellow Muslim.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 60, verse 10–11:

﴿When the believing women come to you as emigrants, test them.﴾ He called them believers (mu’minat) because of their affirmation of faith with their tongues and their uttering the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahada), and nothing appeared from them that contradicted that. Or it is because they are approaching the firm establishment of their faith through testing. ﴿Test them﴾: try them by oath-taking and by examining the indications, so that your assumption of the truth of their faith prevails. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say to the woman being tested: "By Allah, besides whom there is no god, you did not leave out of hatred for a husband. By Allah, you did not leave out of desire to turn away from one land to another. By Allah, you did not leave out seeking worldly gain. By Allah, you did not leave except out of love for Allah and His Messenger." [[Narrated by al-Tabarani and al-Tabari through the narration of al-Aghar ibn al-Sabbah from Khalifa ibn Husayn from Abu Bahz al-Asadi, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas was asked, and he mentioned it in a more complete form. Al-Bazzar said: we do not know it from Ibn ʿAbbas except through this route. ʿAbd al-Razzaq narrated it from Maʿmar from Qatada as a mursal report.]] ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾ than you, because you cannot acquire knowledge of it by which your souls would be at rest, even if you make them swear and examine their conditions, whereas with Allah is the true reality of knowledge of it. ﴿If you know them to be believers﴾, with the knowledge your capacity reaches, which is the prevailing assumption through oath-taking and the appearance of indications, ﴿then do not return them to the unbelievers﴾, that is, do not send them back to their polytheist husbands, ﴿for they are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them [the husbands]﴾ [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: they are not lawful for one another, the believing woman and the polytheist." Ahmad said: This verse is among those cited as evidence for the address of unbelievers regarding the subsidiary rulings (al-furuʿ), because He, exalted, said: "they are not lawful for them" (lahunna hillun lahum), where the first pronoun refers to the believing women and the second to the unbelievers, and the intended meaning is that they are forbidden to the unbelievers, because its counterpart is agreed upon to mean the prohibition of unbelievers for believing women; so each of the two groups, the believing women and the unbelievers, is addressed with the prohibition. Since the doctrine attributed to the companions of Abu Hanifa is that unbelievers are not addressed by the rulings, al-Zamakhshari interprets the verse in a way that agrees with that, taking it to mean the general negation of lawfulness between the believing woman and the unbelievER, so that the prohibition is not attributed exclusively to the unbeliever. This is not a sound escape, for the negated lawfulness between the believing woman and the unbeliever, being a prohibition, must relate to the act of one of them or both; if it relates to the act of each of them—namely, the woman's yielding and the man's intercourse—then the address of the unbeliever with the prohibition is established; and if it relates to the woman's act alone, to the exclusion of the man's act, the structure of the verse rejects that, for it negates lawfulness from both sides together; and if it were so, the words "nor are they lawful for them" would have sufficed. The verification according to the principles of jurisprudence is what we shall mention, God willing: We say: the lawfulness is negated from the act of each of the believing woman and the unbeliever according to the appropriate interpretation. As for the act of the believing woman, which is her yielding, there is no doubt that prohibition attaches to her by the Law, in that she is addressed not to bring about its occurrence in existence in a manner which, if it occurred, would make her liable to punishment for its occurrence. As for the act of the unbeliever, which is intercourse for example, its lawfulness is negated on the ground that the Law intends that intercourse not occur, because of the corruption it involves, and the Law intends that corruptions not take place; the unbeliever is not the object of address, but the imams or those who stand in their stead are addressed to prevent the unbeliever, so that this act involving corruption in the view of the Law does not occur. Thus both acts, from the side of the woman and the man, are a matter the Law desires not to occur; but the object of address involving freedom from corruption, with respect to the woman, is herself, and with respect to the unbeliever, the imams for example. The disputants about addressing unbelievers agree that the Law has an aim that corruptions not come into existence. Do you not see that if an unbeliever openly spreads corruption among Muslims, it is agreed that he must be restrained and prevented from it, and that this is only because of what is understood from the Law's seeking the preservation of existence from corruptions; and the object of the address restraining the unbeliever from openly spreading corruption includes the imams. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] ﴿And give them what they have spent﴾, that is, give their husbands the like of what they paid as bridal gifts (mahr). This was because the treaty of al-Hudaybiyya stipulated that whoever came to you from the people of Mecca would be returned to them, and whoever came to Mecca from you would not be returned to you. They wrote this in a document and sealed it. Subay'a bint al-Harith al-Aslamiyya came as a Muslim while the Prophet (ﷺ) was at al-Hudaybiyya, and her husband Musafir al-Makhzumi came. It is also said it was Sayfi ibn al-Rahib, who said: "O Muhammad, return my wife to me, for you stipulated for us that you would return to us whoever came to you from us, and the clay of this document has not yet dried." So this was revealed as an explanation, because the stipulation was only concerning men, not women. [[Thus al-Baghawi reported it from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain.]]

From al-Dahhak: There was a covenant between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the polytheists: that no woman would come to you from us who is not upon your religion except that you return her to us; and if she enters your religion and has a husband, she is to be returned to her husband who spent upon her. The Prophet (ﷺ) had a similar condition. From Qatada: then this ruling and this covenant were abrogated by the Repudiation (Bara'a), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made her swear, and she swore, and her husband was given what he had spent, and ʿUmar married her.

If you say: how did He call assumption "knowledge" in His words ﴿if you know them﴾? I say: as a notification that the prevailing assumption and what leads to it through effort (ijtihad) and analogy (qiyas) takes the place of knowledge, and that its holder is not included in His words ﴿and do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. If you say: what is the benefit of His words ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾, when that is known without any doubt? I say: its benefit is to make clear that there is no way for you to attain that which would settle the soul and content the breast, namely full comprehension of the reality of their faith, for that is among what the Knower of the unseen has kept to Himself; and that the knowledge which the testing leads to is sufficient for that, and that your obligation does not exceed it. Then He removed from them blame for marrying these emigrant women when they give them their wages (ujur), that is, their bridal gifts (mahr), because the mahr is the wage of intimacy. It is not free of one of two possibilities: either it is meant to be what was given to them so that they would hand it to their husbands, in which case permission to marry them is conditioned on paying it first; or it is meant that if it was given to them as a loan and they then married on that basis, there is no harm; or it is meant to clarify to them that what was given to their husbands does not substitute for the mahr, and that a bridal gift must be paid. Abu Hanifa used this as evidence that if one of the spouses leaves the abode of war as a Muslim or under protection while the other remains a combatant, separation occurs; and he does not require a waiting period (ʿidda) for the emigrant woman and permits marrying her unless she is pregnant. ﴿And do not hold on to the marriage bonds with unbelieving women﴾. The ʿisma is what one holds to by a contract or a cause; the meaning: keep away from them, and let there be no bond of marriage or tie of wedlock between you and them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever has an unbelieving wife in Mecca, let him not count her among his wives, because the difference of the two abodes cut off her bond with him. From al-Nakhaʿi: it refers to the Muslim woman who joins the abode of war and disbelieves.

From Mujahid: He commanded them to divorce the remaining wives who were with the unbelievers and to separate from them. ﴿And ask for what you spent﴾ from the bridal gifts of your wives who have joined the unbelievers, ﴿and let them ask for what they spent﴾ from the bridal gifts of their wives who emigrated. It was recited:

"wa la tumsikū" with the light form; "wa la tummasakū" with the heavy form; "wa la tamassakū", that is: "and do not cling to."

﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges among you﴾: a new sentence; or it is a circumstantial clause from "the judgment of Allah", with the pronoun omitted, meaning: Allah judges it; or the judgment is made to judge by way of emphasis. It is reported that when this verse was revealed, the believers paid what they had been commanded regarding the bridal gifts of the emigrant women to their polytheist husbands, while the polytheists refused to pay anything of the bridal gifts of the unbelieving women to their Muslim husbands. Then the words were revealed: ﴿And if any of your wives have gone from you to the unbelievers﴾, that is, escaped and got away from you, ﴿and you then have a turn﴾: one of them has gone to the unbelievers, and this is in the recitation of Ibn Masʿud: "one" (ahad). If you say: is there any benefit in placing "shay'" (thing) in this position? I say: yes, the benefit is that nothing of this kind is left unrequited, however small and insignificant, as an intensification and strengthening of this ruling. ﴿Then you have a turn (faʿaqabtum)﴾: from ʿuqba, which is the turn, meaning reprisal (tawba), likening what was ruled upon the Muslims and the unbelievers, of paying bridal gifts for these women at one time and those at another, to a matter in which they take turns, as they take turns in riding and other things. Its meaning: the turn of paying the mahr has come to you, so give the one whose wife went to the unbelievers the like of her mahr from the mahr of the emigrant woman, and do not give it to her unbelieving husband. Likewise from al-Zuhri: he gives from the dowry of the one who joined them. It was recited: "fa-aʿqabtum", "fa-ʿaqqabtum" (heavy), "fa-ʿaqabtum" (light), with the qaf open and with it kasra. The meaning of "aʿqabtum" is: you entered into a turn (ʿuqba); "ʿaqqabtum" is from ʿaqibuhu, when one follows him from behind, because each of those taking turns follows the other; likewise "ʿaqabtum" (light), it is said: ʿaqabahu yaʿqubuhu; and "ʿaqabtum" is like "tabiʿtum". Al-Zajjaj said: "fa-ʿaqabtum" means you struck them in battle with a punishment until you took booty; the one whose wife went away was given the mahr from the booty. Others read it so that the turn becomes yours, meaning victory belongs to you until you took booty.

It is said: all of the believing women who emigrated and joined the polytheists and were reverted from Islam were six women: Umm al-Hakam bint Abi Sufyan, who was under ʿIyad ibn Shaddad al-Fihri; Fatima bint Abi Umayya, who was under ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and was the sister of Umm Salama; Buru' bint ʿUqba, who was under Shammas ibn ʿUthman; ʿAbda bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzza ibn Nasla, whose husband was ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd; Hind bint Abi Jahl, who was under Hisham ibn al-ʿAs; and Kulthum bint Jarwal, who was under ʿUmar. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them the mahr of their husbands from the booty. [[Thus al-Tha'labi then al-Baghawi reported it from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain of narration.]]

So this was revealed as an explanation, because the stipulation was only concerning men, not women. [[Thus al-Baghawi reported it from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain.]]

From al-Dahhak: There was a covenant between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the polytheists: that no woman would come to you from us who is not upon your religion except that you return her to us; and if she enters your religion and has a husband, she is to be returned to her husband who spent upon her. The Prophet (ﷺ) had a similar condition. From Qatada: then this ruling and this covenant were abrogated by the Repudiation (Bara'a), so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made her swear, and she swore, and her husband was given what he had spent, and ʿUmar married her.

If you say: how did He call assumption "knowledge" in His words ﴿if you know them﴾? I say: as a notification that the prevailing assumption and what leads to it through effort (ijtihad) and analogy (qiyas) takes the place of knowledge, and that its holder is not included in His words ﴿and do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. If you say: what is the benefit of His words ﴿Allah knows best their faith﴾, when that is known without any doubt? I say: its benefit is to make clear that there is no way for you to attain that which would settle the soul and content the breast, namely full comprehension of the reality of their faith, for that is among what the Knower of the unseen has kept to Himself; and that the knowledge which the testing leads to is sufficient for that, and that your obligation does not exceed it. Then He removed from them blame for marrying these emigrant women when they give them their wages (ujur), that is, their bridal gifts (mahr), because the mahr is the wage of intimacy. It is not free of one of two possibilities: either it is meant to be what was given to them so that they would hand it to their husbands, in which case permission to marry them is conditioned on paying it first; or it is meant that if it was given to them as a loan and they then married on that basis, there is no harm; or it is meant to clarify to them that what was given to their husbands does not substitute for the mahr, and that a bridal gift must be paid. Abu Hanifa used this as evidence that if one of the spouses leaves the abode of war as a Muslim or under protection while the other remains a combatant, separation occurs; and he does not require a waiting period (ʿidda) for the emigrant woman and permits marrying her unless she is pregnant. ﴿And do not hold on to the marriage bonds with unbelieving women﴾. The ʿisma is what one holds to by a contract or a cause; the meaning: keep away from them, and let there be no bond of marriage or tie of wedlock between you and them. Ibn ʿAbbas said: whoever has an unbelieving wife in Mecca, let him not count her among his wives, because the difference of the two abodes cut off her bond with him. From al-Nakhaʿi: it refers to the Muslim woman who joins the abode of war and disbelieves.

From Mujahid: He commanded them to divorce the remaining wives who were with the unbelievers and to separate from them. ﴿And ask for what you spent﴾ from the bridal gifts of your wives who have joined the unbelievers, ﴿and let them ask for what they spent﴾ from the bridal gifts of their wives who emigrated. It was recited:

"wa la tumsikū" with the light form; "wa la tummasakū" with the heavy form; "wa la tamassakū", that is: "and do not cling to."

﴿That is the judgment of Allah; He judges among you﴾: a new sentence; or it is a circumstantial clause from "the judgment of Allah", with the pronoun omitted, meaning: Allah judges it; or the judgment is made to judge by way of emphasis. It is reported that when this verse was revealed, the believers paid what they had been commanded regarding the bridal gifts of the emigrant women to their polytheist husbands, while the polytheists refused to pay anything of the bridal gifts of the unbelieving women to their Muslim husbands. Then the words were revealed: ﴿And if any of your wives have gone from you to the unbelievers﴾, that is, escaped and got away from you, ﴿and you then have a turn﴾: one of them has gone to the unbelievers, and this is in the recitation of Ibn Masʿud: "one" (ahad). If you say: is there any benefit in placing "shay'" (thing) in this position? I say: yes, the benefit is that nothing of this kind is left unrequited, however small and insignificant, as an intensification and strengthening of this ruling. ﴿Then you have a turn (faʿaqabtum)﴾: from ʿuqba, which is the turn, meaning reprisal (tawba), likening what was ruled upon the Muslims and the unbelievers, of paying bridal gifts for these women at one time and those at another, to a matter in which they take turns, as they take turns in riding and other things. Its meaning: the turn of paying the mahr has come to you, so give the one whose wife went to the unbelievers the like of her mahr from the mahr of the emigrant woman, and do not give it to her unbelieving husband. Likewise from al-Zuhri: he gives from the dowry of the one who joined them. It was recited: "fa-aʿqabtum", "fa-ʿaqqabtum" (heavy), "fa-ʿaqabtum" (light), with the qaf open and with it kasra. The meaning of "aʿqabtum" is: you entered into a turn (ʿuqba); "ʿaqqabtum" is from ʿaqibuhu, when one follows him from behind, because each of those taking turns follows the other; likewise "ʿaqabtum" (light), it is said: ʿaqabahu yaʿqubuhu; and "ʿaqabtum" is like "tabiʿtum". Al-Zajjaj said: "fa-ʿaqabtum" means you struck them in battle with a punishment until you took booty; the one whose wife went away was given the mahr from the booty. Others read it so that the turn becomes yours, meaning victory belongs to you until you took booty.

It is said: all of the believing women who emigrated and joined the polytheists and were reverted from Islam were six women: Umm al-Hakam bint Abi Sufyan, who was under ʿIyad ibn Shaddad al-Fihri; Fatima bint Abi Umayya, who was under ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and was the sister of Umm Salama; Buru' bint ʿUqba, who was under Shammas ibn ʿUthman; ʿAbda bint ʿAbd al-ʿUzza ibn Nasla, whose husband was ʿAmr ibn ʿAbd Wudd; Hind bint Abi Jahl, who was under Hisham ibn al-ʿAs; and Kulthum bint Jarwal, who was under ʿUmar. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them the mahr of their husbands from the booty. [[Thus al-Tha'labi then al-Baghawi reported it from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain of narration.]]

And they shall not kill their children. It is also read yaqtulna, with the doubled (intensive) form, meaning the burying alive of daughters (wa'd al-banat).

And they shall not bring a slander which they have invented between their hands and their feet. A woman would pick up a newborn and say to her husband: "This is my child by you."

He used the slander invented "between her hands and feet" as a metaphor for the child she attributes falsely to her husband, because the belly in which she carries it is "between the hands," and the womb from which she delivers it is "between the legs."

And they shall not disobey you in what is right (ma'ruf): in what you command them of good deeds and forbid them from ugly deeds. It was also said: whatever accords with the obedience of God is ma'ruf. If you say: if He had limited Himself to "and they shall not disobey you," would it not be known that the Messenger of God ﷺ commands only what is right? I say: by this He draws attention to the fact that obeying a created being in disobedience to the Creator deserves the utmost caution and avoidance.

It is reported that the Messenger of God ﷺ, when he finished on the day of the conquest of Mecca with the pledge of allegiance from the men, began the pledge of allegiance from the women, while he was on al-Safa [[I have not seen it in this full form, but al-Tabari recorded it in its meaning, and more specifically through al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded it through Muqatil ibn Hayyan. In it is the saying of Hind: "We raised them as children and you killed them as adults," and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, laughed until he fell on his back.]], while 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, was below him, pledging them on his behalf and conveying his words to them, and Hind bint 'Utba, the wife of Abu Sufyan, was veiled and disguised out of fear that the Messenger of God ﷺ would recognize her [[His saying "out of fear that the Messenger of God ﷺ would recognize her" refers to what she had done to Hamza, as in al-Nasafi, and that was at the battle of Uhud. (Al-'Ali)]]. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "I pledge you that you will not associate anything with God." Hind raised her head and said: "By God, we used to worship idols, and you are taking from us a matter you have never taken from the men; you take the pledge of the men for Islam and jihad." He, peace be upon him, said: "And that you will not steal." [[His saying "peace be upon him, and that they will not steal" — in al-Nasafi, before this: 'Umar pledged the women that they would not associate anything with God. (Al-'Ali)]] She said: "Abu Sufyan is a stingy man, and I have taken some of his wealth, some trifles, and I do not know whether it is lawful for me or not." Abu Sufyan said: "Whatever you have taken in the past and in the future is lawful for you." The Messenger of God ﷺ laughed, recognized her, and said to her: "Are you indeed Hind bint 'Utba?" She said: "Yes. So pardon what has passed, O Prophet of God; may God pardon you." He said: "And that they will not commit adultery." She said: "Does a free woman commit adultery?" In another narration: no woman among them had ever committed adultery. He, peace be upon him, said: "And that they will not kill their children." She said: "We raised them as children and you killed them as adults; you and they know best." Her son Handhala ibn Abi Sufyan had been killed on the day of Badr. 'Umar laughed until he fell on his back, and the Messenger of God ﷺ smiled. He said: "And that they will not bring a slander." She said: "By God, slander is an ugly matter, and you command us only to rectitude and noble character." He said: "And that they will not disobey you in what is right." She said: "By God, we did not sit in this gathering of ours with the intention of disobeying you in anything."

It was said regarding the manner of the pledge: he called for a vessel of water, dipped his hand in it, and then they dipped their hands in it [[Reported by Ibn Sa'd from al-Waqidi from Usama ibn Zayd from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb in similar wording; it has a witness in al-Tabarani from 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud, and another in Ta'rikh Asbahan of Abu Nu'aym under the letter ha', from the hadith of Asma' bint Yazid.]]. It was also said that he shook hands with them, and there was a Qatari cloth on his hand [[Reported by Abu Dawud in al-Maradil from al-Sha'bi: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ pledged the women, a Qatari cloak was brought and he placed it on his hand, and said: I do not shake hands with women." 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from al-Thawri from Mansur from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ used to shake hands with women with a Qatari cloth on his hand."]]. It was also said that 'Umar shook hands with them on his behalf [[Recorded by Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la, al-Tabari and others from the hadith of Umm 'Atiyya, who said: "When the Messenger of God ﷺ arrived in Medina, he commanded the women of the Ansar, gathered them in a house, and then sent 'Umar to them. 'Umar came and greeted them—" and she related the story, in which: "Then he extended his hand from outside the house, and we extended our hands from inside the house."]].

It is related that some of the poor among the Muslims used to befriend the Jews in order to obtain some of their fruits.

[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "A group of weak Muslims had allied themselves with the Jews in order to obtain some of their produce, so this verse was revealed; and what is meant by the disbelievers is the polytheists... etc."] Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Al-Zamakhshari had mentioned, regarding His words ﴿And the two seas are not alike﴾ up to His words ﴿and from each you eat tender flesh﴾, that the end of the verse is an digression (istitrad), which is a type of rhetorical art (fann min funun al-bayan) that has a designated chapter in it among its specialists. This verse of Surah al-Mumtahanah can very well be of this art, for it censures the Jews and then digresses to censure the polytheists through a fine kind of association. Eloquent speakers can find nothing better or more fitting for digression than this. Among the verses with which they have introduced this art is the poet's saying:

"If a youth fears God and obeys Him, there is no harm in him even if he has committed a sin."

And his saying: "If you are lying, the one who has told me, then you have escaped as al-Harith ibn Hisham escaped."

"He abandoned his beloved rather than fight in their defence, and escaped with the head of his swift horse and its bridle."

It was said to them: ﴿Do not take as allies a people upon whom Allah has brought His anger﴾, ﴿for they have despaired of the Hereafter, just as the disbelievers have despaired of those in the graves﴾ — that is, of their rising and returning to life — because of their obstinacy toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while they know that he is the Messenger described in the Torah.

It was also said that ﴿of the companions of the graves﴾ is an explanation of "the disbelievers", meaning: just as the disbelievers who are in the graves have despaired of the good of the Hereafter, since they have clearly seen the ugliness of their state and the evil of their final destination.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Mumtahanah will have the believing men and believing women as intercessors on the Day of Resurrection."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi with their chains to Ubayy ibn Ka'b (may Allah be pleased with him).] ..
